chunks.text:
What is Datawrap?
Datawrap moves data between systems and shows you whether it arrived intact. Transfer Studio maps columns across systems and runs preflight gates before any write: nine core gates plus the policy gates each route needs. After the write it reads the destination back and compares it with the source. Schedules, Pilot, and MCP use the same engine.

Product surfaces (sidebar map)
The sidebar in the signed-in workspace matches these guides. Start in Transfer Studio, then move on to Schedules, Contracts, Pilot, and MCP.
Platform — Overview, Transfer, Connectors, Contracts, Exit readiness
Operations — Jobs (Job space), Schedules, Transforms, Library, Query, Pilot
System — Settings (SSO and Team), MCP, Help, Proofs
The path every load takes — Source → Destination → Transform → Map → Validate → Run → Job space
Overview, with the Platform, Operations, and System sidebar used in every guide.

Your first transfer (step by step)
Follow this path in the signed-in workspace. Every screenshot comes from the hosted product.
Confirm the workspace is healthy
Open **Overview** and check throughput, migration health, and recent jobs. If the panels fail to load, fix connectivity with a workspace admin before you create connections.
Where: Sidebar → Overview
Add or test a connector
Open **Platform → Connectors**. Click **New connection** to add a source or destination, or click **Test** on an existing row and check that **Last test** shows passed.
Where: Platform → Connectors → New connection
Run Transfer Studio Source → Destination → Transform → Map → Validate → Run
Open **Platform → Transfer** (or **New transfer**). On **Source**, pick a **Database** connection and a table, and check the source schema. Then continue through **Destination**, **Transform** (click **Continue without transforming** when there is no recipe), **Map**, and **Validate**.

Fix every blocked gate before **Run**. On Validate the footer holds the one primary action: the fix for the blocking gate, or **Execute** when the decision is approve. The Transfer Studio guide walks through a full Postgres to Snowflake load.
Where: Platform → Transfer  ·  or New transfer
Prove the load in Job space
Open **Operations → Jobs** and select the run. The **Trust Report** reads the destination back and compares it with the source: rows in each, rows that differ, and the checksum per table. Open **Reversibility** if the route must be able to give the source values back. Neither is an exactly-once certificate; delivery is at-least-once.
Where: Operations → Jobs → Trust Report

Workspace concepts
Every transfer runs inside a workspace with connectors, saved routes, synonym dictionaries, and audit history. Team members inherit RBAC from your IdP in enterprise tenants.
Connectors — encrypted credentials scoped to workspace
Saved routes — reuse mapping + write mode presets
Synonym dictionary — accepted semantic pairs for auto-map
Job space — run history with the Trust Report, reversibility, quarantine, and sign-off

What your organization receives
Datawrap is delivered as a **hosted enterprise workspace** at your tenant URL (for example `your-company.datawrap.io`). After sign-in you work entirely in the browser — there is nothing to install on operator laptops.

The signed-in product includes **Overview**, **Connectors**, **Transfer Studio**, **Schedules**, **Jobs** (Job space), **Query**, **Pilot**, and **Settings**. Your IT team configures SSO and optional BYOK once; day-to-day operators create connections, run governed transfers, and prove loads.
After SSO, Overview shows throughput, migration health, and recent jobs for your workspace.

Procedure: get access
Use this path when onboarding a new operator or confirming a newly provisioned tenant. Complete every step before you create production connectors.
Receive your tenant URL and role
A workspace **admin** (or Datawrap provisioning) invites you by email with one of three roles:

**Viewer** — read Jobs, quarantine, and Trust Reports; cannot create connectors or run transfers.

**Editor** — create connectors, run **Transfer Studio** and **Schedules**, and open **Job space**. Only an Admin adds, removes or re-roles members.

**Admin** — everything Editors can do, plus **Settings → SSO**, **Enterprise**, **BYOK**, **Team** roles, and API keys. There is no Owner role in the product.

Open the invite link, or go directly to your tenant URL (for example `https://your-company.datawrap.io`). Sign in with your company identity provider — **Okta**, **Azure AD / Entra ID**, **Google Workspace**, or another SAML 2.0 / OIDC IdP configured for the tenant.
Where: IT / Datawrap admin → invite email
Sign in with SSO
On the login screen choose **Continue with SSO** (or your company's branded SSO button). Authenticate with your work account. Datawrap issues a workspace session that inherits your RBAC role from the invite or from IdP group claims.

A successful sign-in lands on **Overview**. Confirm the top bar shows your **workspace** name (switcher, when you belong to more than one) and that the left sidebar lists **Platform** (Transfer, Connectors, Contracts) and **Operations** (Jobs, Schedules). If you only see a blank or permission error, stop and ask a workspace admin to verify your role under **Settings → Team**.
Where: Login → Continue with SSO
Confirm you can reach Connectors and Transfer
In the left sidebar open **Platform → Connectors**. You should see the connections table, empty or with existing rows. Then open **Platform → Transfer** (Transfer Studio) or click **New transfer** if shown.

You are ready for day-one work when:

**1.** **New connection** is visible on Connectors (Editors and Admins).

**2.** Transfer Studio opens the **Source → Destination → Transform → Map → Validate → Run** wizard.

**3.** **Operations → Jobs** opens Job space for past and live runs.

If Connectors or Transfer is missing from the sidebar, your role is likely **Viewer** — ask a workspace admin to raise it to **Editor** under **Settings → Team**.
Where: Sidebar → Platform → Connectors  ·  Transfer
Tip: **Viewer** — inspect Jobs and proof only. **Editor** — run transfers and manage connectors (members are managed by an Admin). **Admin** — SSO, BYOK, Team roles, and enterprise controls under **Settings**. Switching workspace in the top bar (or on Team) is live for every Settings tab.

Admin checklist (workspace admins)
Workspace **admins** complete these once per workspace. Operators do not need this checklist to run day-to-day transfers — it is for IT and security readiness.
**Settings → SSO** — choose SAML or OIDC, paste IdP metadata URL (or upload XML), map roles if your IdP sends group claims, then click **Test login** and **Save**.
**Settings → Enterprise** — set tenant display name, data **region**, session timeout, and (for a tenant custom domain) an optional IP allowlist. The workspace picker here is the same live workspace as Team.
**Settings → Enterprise → BYOK** — upload your customer KMS key when procurement requires customer-managed encryption for connector secrets.
**Settings → Team** — invite Viewers, Editors, and Admins with least privilege; re-check IdP group → role mapping after SSO setup. Member and login lists refresh while the tab is open.
**Settings → Security** — download the **Security posture report** for SOC 2 / GDPR / HIPAA questionnaires. Controls are implemented; no third-party certificate is claimed.
Tip: If your tenant URL is not live yet, email **sales@datawrap.io**. Provisioning is handled by Datawrap — operators never install or run a local API.

Supported browsers & network
Use a current **Chromium**, **Firefox**, or **Safari** build. Connector **Test** and transfers need outbound network access from the Datawrap worker (in your pinned region) to your sources and destinations — databases, warehouses, and object stores.

Corporate proxies and firewalls must allow those destinations for the workspace region selected under **Settings → Enterprise**. If **Test** fails with a timeout while credentials are correct, open a ticket with network/security before re-running Validate gates in Transfer Studio.

chunks.section_title: Example transfer used in this guide
chunks.text:
Example transfer used in this guide
Every screenshot below comes from one real session in the hosted workspace.

**Source:** **Orders Postgres (demo)**, table `public.sales_orders`: 5,100 rows, 11 columns (`order_id`, `region`, `store_code`, `product_sku`, `units`, `unit_price`, `discount_pct`, `order_total`, `status`, `ordered_at`, `attributes`).

**Destination:** **Warehouse Snowflake (demo)**, database `DW_DEMO`, table `SALES_ORDERS_REPORTING`. The table did not exist before the run.

**Sync mode:** **Full append** with manual approval and strict validation.

**Result:** 11 of 11 columns mapped, 17 gates passed with 6 not applicable, 5,100 rows written, and a full checksum match in Job space.

Schedules, Pilot, and MCP use the same six steps. None of them can skip a gate or the read-back.

Procedure: load sales_orders into Snowflake
Follow the six steps in order. The numbered markers on each screenshot point at the control the step talks about.
Step 1 — Source: pick the table
Open **Transfer** in the sidebar or click **New transfer**. The rail across the top shows the six steps: **Source**, **Destination**, **Transform**, **Map**, **Validate**, **Run**.

Under **Where is your data?** choose **Database**. Pick **Orders Postgres (demo)** as the source connector, keep **Table** as the extract, and choose `sales_orders`.

The **Source schema** panel on the right lists the 11 columns with their types and shows sample rows. Check it before you continue: that profile is what Map and Validate work from. Then click **Continue to Destination**.
Where: Sidebar → Transfer  ·  or New transfer
Tip: Choose **SQL query** as the extract to load the result of a SELECT instead of a whole table. It goes through the same Map and Validate steps.
Step 2 — Destination: pick the warehouse and table
On **Destination** keep **Warehouse** selected and pick **Warehouse Snowflake (demo)** from **Saved connections**. Under **Target location** set the database to `DW_DEMO` and the table to `SALES_ORDERS_REPORTING`.

Because the table does not exist yet, the page says **Table not found: Datawrap will create it automatically on first write**. Nothing is created now. The DDL is shown for approval in Validate.

**Sync defaults** shows the mode for this run: **Full append**, manual approval, strict validation. Open **Advanced** for overwrite, incremental, CDC, SCD Type 2, mirror, cursor, and drift settings. Click **Continue to Transform**.
Where: Destination → Warehouse → saved connection → target location
Tip: File export is not available on the hosted cloud. Use a warehouse, database, or object-store connection as the destination.
Step 3 — Transform: add a recipe or skip it
Transform is where a pre-load recipe lives: rename, round, filter, or apply rules from the **Transform Library**. If you add steps, Validate checks the transformed rows rather than the raw source.

This example loads the table as it is, so click **Continue without transforming**.
Where: Transform → Continue without transforming
Step 4 — Map: review every column
**Map columns** pairs each source column with a destination name and type. Here the header reads **11 of 11 mapped · 11 ready to approve**. `order_id` stays `BIGINT`, the text columns become `VARCHAR`, and the decimals keep their precision as `NUMBER(10,2)`, `NUMBER(5,2)`, and `NUMBER(12,2)`.

Use **Needs attention** to see only the rows that need a decision. Expand a row to see why it was mapped that way. The JSON column `attributes` becomes `VARIANT` in Snowflake, and the expanded row says the conversion keeps every value.

Click **Approve eligible (11)**, then **Continue to Validate**. Pairs that look alike but mean different things, such as quantity and amount, are never approved in bulk. You confirm or remap them one by one.
Where: Map columns → Approve eligible → Continue to Validate
Tip: **More → Open mapping proof** shows the confidence and fidelity evidence for each pair before you validate.
Step 5 — Validate: clear every blocking gate
Validate runs every gate the route needs. On this route that is 23: the nine core gates plus policy gates for population fit, DDL, staging, sync contract, column coverage, and field reduction.

The first run blocked on one gate: **Create destination table**. The table does not exist, and strict validation will not create a table nobody approved. The card shows the exact `CREATE TABLE` statement, and the footer's primary button becomes **Approve destination DDL**.

After approving and re-running, the summary reads **APPROVE · 17 passed · 0 blocked gates · 6 skipped** in 107.7 seconds. The six skipped gates do not apply to a new table with no code crosswalk. **Type coercions in sample** lists 25 JSON values that will be written as `VARIANT`, none quarantined.

**Execute** unlocks only when no gate is blocked and the decision is approve. The headline still says **not migration proven**: that comes from the read-back after the write.
Where: Validate footer → the one primary action
Tip: To see each gate on its own, scroll to **Validation rules**. The Preflight gates guide explains each gate ID.
Step 6 — Run: execute and watch the load
Click **Execute**. Run shows the phases (**Extract**, **Transform**, **Load**, **Reconcile**), rows read and written, and a live event log.

When it finishes, the append check compares the destination before and after: **0 before, 5,100 after, 5,100 appended**, and the delta balances. Open the job in **Job space** for the Trust Report, which reads Snowflake back and compares it with Postgres.
Where: Validate → Execute  ·  then Job space
Tip: Delivery is at-least-once. A retried append can write a batch twice, so use an upsert mode with a business key when duplicates matter.

Write modes (Advanced)
Open **Advanced** on Destination to set the sync mode. Schedules offer the same modes on every run.
**Full append** — keep existing rows and append the full snapshot (used in this example).
**Full overwrite** — replace the target, then load.
**Incremental append** — new rows only, by cursor.
**Incremental deduped** — cursor plus primary-key upserts.
**CDC** — log-based changes when the source supports it. Delivery is at-least-once upsert unless a route proves otherwise.
**SCD Type 2 / Mirror** — history and mirror modes; a primary key is required where noted.
**Destination write → Query** — one INSERT, MERGE, or UPDATE with `:binds` mapped to source columns. Failed rows go to quarantine. Not CDC.
**Destination write → Stored procedure** — one CALL or EXEC per row. SQLite has no destination procedures; a destination query INSERT is allowed.

chunks.section_title: After Run: quarantine and the Trust Report
chunks.text:
After Run: quarantine and the Trust Report
Rows that fail a type or policy check go to quarantine with the **column**, **value**, and **reason**. They are never dropped quietly. After the write, Datawrap reads the destination back and compares counts and checksums with the source. The Trust Report shows the result: for this run, 5,100 rows on each side, 0 that differ, and a full checksum match.
Tip: Open **Jobs → select the run → Trust Report** before you sign off. **Report (.md)** downloads the evidence for an audit file.
Job space: the Trust Report for the sales_orders load.

When Validate runs
Validate runs in Transfer Studio, and the same gates run again before every scheduled run. Execute stays locked until the decision is approve. A pass that still needs review does not unlock the write.
Tip: Schedules cannot skip Validate. A failing gate on a schedule blocks the write the same way it blocks a manual run, and the schedule parks with the reason.

Core gates (before write)
Every route runs these nine. Open any card under **Validation rules** for the rule text and what to change.
G1 Source readable — source connects and rows can be read
G2 Destination write access — destination is reachable with write/create privilege
G3 Schema contract — source and target schemas are compatible
G4 Column mappings — every column maps above the confidence threshold
G5 Sample dry-run — sample rows pass the same transforms writers use
G6 Target DDL — required CREATE / ALTER statements are valid
G7 Staging capacity — destination has headroom for the volume
G8 Sample reconciliation — pre-write sample identity and uniqueness hold (post-load checksum runs after Execute)
G9 Data integrity — encoding, required nulls, identity duplicates, precision on the sample
Validation rules on the sales_orders route: 23 gates, 17 passed (green) and 6 not applicable (grey).

Policy & drift gates
Validate adds gates for the sync mode, the destination, and your Advanced settings. A gate that does not apply to the route shows as skipped, not passed. On the example route 14 policy gates were added; 8 passed and 6 did not apply.
G3F Population fit — values fit bounded destination types such as DECIMAL(p,s) and VARCHAR(n), checked on the rows this run holds
G6C Create destination table — a table that does not exist is created only after you approve its DDL
G10 Schema change policy — detected drift is allowed by the route's policy
G11 Validation posture — the run matches the posture you chose (strict in the example)
G12 Sync contract — the cursor and primary key satisfy the sync mode
G12S Staging policy — staging tables and their cleanup follow the workspace staging policy
G13 Source column coverage — every source column is mapped or declared an intentional omission; an unaccounted column blocks instead of being dropped
G16 Field reduction governance — every source column not carried over has a recorded reason, and a reason the sample disproves blocks
G14, G15, G19, G20, G21, G22 — required columns, existing-table shape, schema replacement, code crosswalk, control totals, and referential integrity; they apply when the destination or contract calls for them
G24R Reversibility — added when the route must stay reversible; blocks Execute if any column cannot give the source value back

Procedure: fix a blocked gate
Use this path whenever Validate shows a red or blocking gate.
Open the failing gate card
The summary names the blocking gate. In the example the first run stopped on **Create destination table**: `SALES_ORDERS_REPORTING` did not exist, and the card showed the `CREATE TABLE` statement Datawrap would run. Read the card and note whether the cause is mapping, credentials, capacity, encoding, DDL, or drift.
Where: Transfer Studio → Validate → gate card
Remediate in Map or Advanced
Use the control the card points to. A DDL gate is cleared by approving the statement. A mapping or fidelity gate sends you to **Map** to remap a column or accept an intentional cast. A sync-contract gate sends you to **Destination → Advanced** to set a primary key or cursor. Encoding problems can be stripped or sent to quarantine.
Where: Map · Destination → Advanced · Fix bad data
Re-run until Execute unlocks
Click **Re-run Validate**. Execute unlocks only when the server returns **approve** with no blocked gate. In the example the second run showed 17 passed, 0 blocked, 6 skipped.
Where: Validate → Re-run Validate
Tip: The unlock is decided by the server, not the browser. Editing the page cannot unlock Execute.

Semantic roles
Datawrap detects roles like amount, email, identifier, timestamp, and address — not just string name matching.
Map: each source column with its destination name, type, transform, and status.

Synonym dictionary
Accept or reject mapping suggestions. Accepted pairs enter your workspace synonym dictionary for future auto-maps.
Expand a row to see why it was mapped: here, attributes keeps every JSON value as VARIANT.

Confidence scores
Each pair has a confidence score, shown when you expand the row. Use the **Needs attention** and **Ready** tabs to focus on what needs a decision. Click **Approve** when a pair is right, remap it when it is not, and accept the risk only for a cast you mean to be lossy.

Schema drift detection
Datawrap compares current source and destination schemas against your saved route. Drift shows up in Validate, and a schedule parks with the change before its next run writes anything.
New columns in source — review suggested maps
Removed columns — confirm destination still valid
Type changes — preflight type-coercion gate validates casts

What you see on Connectors
The **Connectors** page is the inventory of every saved source and destination in your workspace. The filters at the top count **All**, **Healthy**, and **Errors**. The table shows each connection's capability, **Last test**, and **Last used**, so you know what is safe to schedule.

Use the **Connections** tab for saved credentials. Use **Catalog** only when browsing available driver types — Catalog does not store secrets.
Connectors: the saved demo connections, each with capability, last test, and last used.

Procedure: add a connector
Follow this path whenever you onboard a new system. Numbered markers on the screenshots match the live product UI.
Open Connectors
In the signed-in workspace, open **Platform → Connectors**. Confirm the **Connections** tab is selected when you are managing saved credentials (not **Catalog**).

If **Errors** is greater than zero, open those rows and re-run **Test** before you schedule anything against them.
Where: Sidebar → Platform → Connectors
Click New connection — Choose a connector dialog
Click **New connection** (top-right). A modal dialog opens: **Choose a connector**.

Use category chips (**Databases**, **Data Warehouses**, **Files & Formats**, …), search, and status filters (**Proven in CI**, **Not yet proven**, **Transfer-ready**, **Source only**, **Test only**, **Planned**). Transfer-ready cards show badges such as **Full Transfer**.

Pick a driver — for example **PostgreSQL**, **MySQL**, **MongoDB**, **Snowflake**, **BigQuery**, **S3**, **CSV / TSV**, or a SQLAlchemy generic. Do not schedule **Planned** catalog entries in production.
Where: Top-right → New connection
Enter credentials and Test
After you pick a driver, the credential form opens (still in the dialog flow). Fill **host**, **database**, and auth (password, key, or cloud credentials). Click **Test** before **Save**. Do not skip Test.

**Test passed** (green) on the Connections table means the driver reached the system, so it is safe to pick in Transfer Studio and Schedules.

**Test failed** (red) means fix credentials, firewall, or region network access before using the connector. Failed connections block Validate gates later.
Where: Wizard form → Test → Save
Tip: Credentials are encrypted at rest with workspace-scoped keys. Enterprise tenants can enable **BYOK** under **Settings → Enterprise**. Passwords never appear in job logs.
Use it in Transfer Studio
Open **Platform → Transfer**. On **Source** (or later **Destination**), choose **Database** or **Cloud storage**. Your saved healthy connectors appear in the picker.

Continue through **Map → Validate → Run**. A green **Test passed** on Connectors does **not** skip preflight — Validate still runs the full gate set before any production write.
Where: Transfer → Source or Destination → Database

Honest transfer-ready labels
Catalog tiles are not the same as production drivers. Each connector shows one of these readiness states. Only routes with transfer-ready evidence get the production badge — everything else stays labelled honestly.
**Certified** — the CI jobs that prove this engine ran green with no skipped test; safe for production schedules after Test passed.
**Proven on an emulator only** — Snowflake and BigQuery: their CI jobs ran green against emulators (fakesnow, the BigQuery emulator), not a real cloud account. The tile says so; prove the route on your own account before relying on it.
**Implemented — not yet proven** — the driver runs transfers, but no green CI run proves its engine yet; not offered for production schedules.
**Source only** — readable; no transfer-ready write path.
**Test only** — auth works; write path is not transfer-ready.
**Planned** — catalog presence only; do not schedule yet.

Native drivers & SQLAlchemy
A connector is **Certified** only when the CI jobs that prove its engine ran green with no skipped test against the real engine (Snowflake and BigQuery are proven on emulators only and labelled that way); an engine that runs but has no such run yet is labelled **Implemented — not yet proven** and is not offered for production schedules. The connector catalog shows each tile's tier. **Redshift** stays Planned until a named PRODUCTION_SKU matrix. Generic **SQLAlchemy** URLs extend reach with the same **Validate** preflight path used by native drivers. Catalog tiles are not transfer-live. Proofs → Integrity ledger has **Run desktop lab**: 80 catalog slots exercised as source and destination when the desktop backend is up. **Run unique-engine matrix** is the live src×dst cartesian (Postgres, MySQL, Mongo, SQL Server, Oracle, object stores, warehouses on emulators). Hosted twins (Neon/RDS/CNPG/OpenShift PostgreSQL) share a driver — that option is real, it is not 80 unique engines.

What a schedule is
A **schedule** runs a route you have already validated in Transfer Studio on a cadence. Each run is a full job: the same gates, quarantine, and read-back as a manual run. Recurring does not mean fewer checks.

When a run hits a finding that needs a person, the schedule **parks** instead of retrying. The **Waiting on a decision** panel at the top of the page says what happened and gives one button to fix it. In the screenshot, `orders_feed` parked because upsert needs a business key, and the button is **Open Transfer Studio**.
Tip: The simplest way to start is from Transfer Studio: after Validate approves a route, click **Schedule** in the footer. A schedule created on this page saves cadence only and stays paused until the route has an approved mapping.
Schedules: four schedules, one parked on a finding rather than retrying it.

Procedure: create a schedule
This path uses the **Create recurring sync** form for the Postgres to Snowflake route from the Transfer Studio guide.
Open Create recurring sync
Open **Operations → Schedules** and click **New schedule**. The page switches to the **Create recurring sync** form, with a **Creating schedule** chip at the top.

Fill in:

1. **Schedule name** (example: `Nightly sales_orders → Snowflake`)
2. **Source connector** and **Source table** (`Orders Postgres (demo)`, `sales_orders`)
3. **Destination connector** and **Destination table** (`Warehouse Snowflake (demo)`, `SALES_ORDERS_REPORTING`)

The source can also be a **SQL query** or a **Procedure**. **Open Transfer Studio** takes the same route to Map and Validate if it has not been approved yet.
Where: Sidebar → Operations → Schedules → New schedule
Tip: If a connector list is empty, add the connection under **Platform → Connectors** first. **Save schedule** stays disabled until both sides are chosen.
Set the cadence and sync mode
In **Cadence** choose **Preset** or **Cron**. The presets are **Hourly**, **Daily**, and **Weekly**. They count from the last run, so Daily means about 24 hours after the previous run, not a fixed time of day. For a fixed time use **Cron** with a timezone, for example `10 10 * * *` for 10:10 every day.

In **Sync mode** pick how rows move: **Full append**, **Full overwrite**, **Incremental append**, **Incremental deduped**, **CDC**, **SCD Type 2**, or **Mirror**. Which ones are offered depends on the two connectors. Upsert, SCD Type 2, and Mirror need a **Primary key**; incremental modes need a **Cursor column**.
Where: Cadence → Preset | Cron  ·  Sync mode
Require reversibility and set retries
Under **Data contract & reversibility** you can bind a signed contract and require it before each run, so an unattended run cannot write against a schema nobody signed. **Require reversibility before each run (fail-closed)** blocks any run where a column could not give the source value back, such as a hash, a mask, or a narrowing cast.

Under **Retry & notifications** set **Max retries**, **Retry backoff (seconds)**, and whether to **Notify on failure** and **Notify on success**. Retries apply to transient failures. A finding that needs a person parks the schedule instead.

Click **Save schedule**. The toast says **Schedule created**, or **Schedule saved paused** if it cannot run yet.
Where: Data contract & reversibility  ·  Retry & notifications
Open the schedule
Click a schedule to open its drawer. **Overview** shows the cadence, sync mode, contract, reversibility requirement, last and next run, and the numbers from the last run: mapped columns, rows changed, quarantined rows, and trust score.

The footer has **Run now**, **Re-sync (full)**, **Last job**, **Activate** or **Pause**, **Edit**, **Export YAML**, and **Delete**. **Edit** reopens the same form.
Where: Click a schedule row → detail drawer
Read the run history
**History** lists each run with its status, time, rows read and written, rows rejected, and the job ID. Copy the job ID or click **Last job** to open the run in **Job space**, where the Trust Report and Reversibility tabs show what that run wrote.

Schedules owns the timing. Job space owns the evidence for each run.
Where: Drawer → History
Tip: Turn on **Notify on failure** before you move a schedule to a production cadence.

Sync modes
Schedules offer the same sync modes as Transfer Studio. Pick the one that matches how the destination should treat repeats and deletes:
**Full overwrite** — replace the target, then load the snapshot
**Full append** — keep existing rows and append the full snapshot
**Incremental append** — new rows only, by cursor
**Incremental deduped** — cursor plus primary-key upserts
**CDC** — log-based changes when the source supports it. Delivery is at-least-once upsert unless a route proves otherwise.
**SCD Type 2** — versioned history (primary key required)
**Mirror** — keys missing from the source are soft-deleted in the destination (`_deleted`), so the physical row count stays the same (primary key required)
Tip: Rows that fail a check go to quarantine. The rest of the batch still lands, and nothing is dropped quietly.

Schedules as YAML
The Schedules toolbar has **Export YAML** and **Import YAML**, and a **Require signed** switch that refuses imported schedules unless their contract is signed. Keep the exported YAML in version control as the reviewable definition of cadence, route, and sync mode.

Redis destination keys
Redis stores each row under `prefix:identity`. Datawrap prefers `id`, `*_id`, or `uuid`, then natural keys (`code`, `iso`, `name`, `sku`). Columns that are not unique, like `capital` or `city`, are never chosen when a stronger key exists. Set **Primary key** in the schedule's sync mode panel (or on Map for a one-off run) to choose the column yourself.

What a contract is
A **data contract** records what a route promises: the columns, their types and nullability, and the mappings that produce them. Contracts live under **Platform → Contracts**. A schedule can require a **signed** contract before each run, so an unattended run cannot write against a shape nobody agreed to.

Each contract also has a **breaker**. Repeated failures open it and stop further runs until the cause is fixed; it closes again after a recovery timeout.
Contracts: one draft, v1, 11 columns and 11 mappings, breaker closed.

chunks.section_title: Procedure: save, sign, and enforce a contract
chunks.text:
Procedure: save, sign, and enforce a contract
This path uses the contract saved from the Postgres to Snowflake route in the Transfer Studio guide.
Save the contract from Validate
When Validate approves a route, the footer offers **Save contract**. It saves the approved columns and mappings as a **Draft**, version **v1**, under **Platform → Contracts**.
Where: Transfer Studio → Validate → Save contract
Review it and sign
Open **Contracts** and click the contract. The drawer shows its status, version, source, and destination, with tabs for **Overview**, **Columns**, **Mappings**, **Quality**, and **History**. **Overview** includes the breaker state and the preflight gates the contract was saved with.

Check **Columns**: for this route, 11 columns from `order_id BIGINT` to `status VARCHAR`, with `unit_price` as `NUMBER(10,2)`. When the owners agree, click **Sign**. **Deprecate** retires a contract; **Export** downloads it.
Where: Contracts → contract row → drawer → Sign
Require it on the schedule
On the schedule form, open **Data contract & reversibility**. Pick the signed contract and turn on the requirement to have it signed before each run. If the contract is unsigned, missing, or the live schema has drifted from it, the run is refused and the schedule parks with the reason, the same way a failed gate would stop it.
Where: Schedules → New schedule or Edit → Data contract & reversibility

What Transforms are
Open **Operations → Transforms**. A transform here is a set of SQL models that runs **at the destination after a transfer lands**, such as a reporting table rebuilt from the rows just loaded. Each row shows the destination, how many models it has, what triggers it, and whether it is enabled.

This is different from the **Transform** step in Transfer Studio, which changes rows before they are written.
Transforms: Revenue by country, one model on Analytics Postgres (demo), enabled.

Open a transform
Click a row to open it. The drawer shows the destination and schema, the trigger (**After transfer** runs it when the named tables land), the bound contract if any, the version, and the models with their build order.

The footer has **Dry run**, which checks the SQL without writing, **Run now**, **Export dbt**, **Edit**, and **Delete**.
Tip: Use **Dry run** after any change to the source route. A model that refers to a renamed column fails here instead of in the next scheduled run.
Revenue by country: runs after transfer and builds revenue_by_country.

chunks.section_title: Pre-load recipes live in the Library
chunks.text:
Pre-load recipes live in the Library
Rules that change rows before the write, such as renames, rounding, and filters, are kept in **Operations → Library** and applied on the Transfer Studio **Transform** step. Validate then checks the transformed rows, and Reversibility flags any step that changes values or drops rows.

When to use Pilot
Open **Operations → Pilot**, or the **Pilot** tab on the right edge of any page. Ask a question about a table on a saved connection. Pilot builds one SQL statement, runs it on the server over the whole table, and shows the SQL and a result reference under the answer.

In the screenshot, Pilot counted 5,100 rows in `sales_orders` and then totalled `order_total` by region for 5 regions. Both answers say they are exact server-side aggregates, not samples.
Pilot: a row count and a group-by on sales_orders, each with its SQL and a result reference.

Changes need your confirmation
Pilot can start work as well as answer questions. Anything that would create a connection, start a transfer, or change a schedule becomes a request you confirm first. After you confirm, it runs through the same Map and Validate gates as Transfer Studio.

Example prompts
Name the table and the connection. Questions that can be answered with one aggregate work best.
How many rows are in sales_orders on Orders Postgres (demo)?
Total order_total by region in sales_orders on Orders Postgres (demo)
Summarize that
What should I do next?
Tip: With the local engine, Pilot handles counts, totals, group-bys, and filters. Open-ended prompts like a full workspace briefing need a configured model under **Settings → AI Models**.

Open the MCP page
Open **System → MCP**. The page shows the **MCP server URL** with its status, setup for **Cursor**, **Claude Desktop**, **VS Code**, a custom GPT, and any other client that speaks MCP over streamable HTTP, and a **Recent activity** list of agent calls. Agents never see connection passwords; they work through the same roles as people.
System → MCP: the server URL, client setup, and recent agent calls.

Agent security
MCP tools follow workspace roles. Agents cannot read connection secrets; they can only start the operations their key allows. Anything that creates or moves data waits for `confirm_action`, and agent runs pass Validate before they write, like every other run.

Open Query Playground
Open **Operations → Query** and pick a saved connection. The schema browser lists tables and columns, the editor knows the connection's SQL dialect, and **Row limit** caps the result (1,000 by default). Each tab keeps its own connection, so you can query the source and the destination side by side.

The screenshot totals paid, shipped, and delivered orders by region on **Warehouse Snowflake (demo)**: 5 rows in 3.1 seconds, with LATAM at 767 orders and 182,648.65 in revenue. The same query on the Postgres source returns the same numbers. Kafka topics and vector stores are not queried here.
Query: revenue by region on the Snowflake copy, with a tab open for the Postgres source.

Tips
Query is **read-only**. Only SELECT, WITH, EXPLAIN, SHOW, DESCRIBE, and similar statements are accepted; DML, DDL, and CALL or EXEC are refused before they reach the database. On PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and Oracle the statement also runs in a read-only transaction. Results can be filtered and copied as CSV, JSON, or Markdown. Writes go through Transfer Studio or Schedules.
A DELETE is refused with the reason, and nothing is sent to the database.

Bridge to Transfer Studio
Query does not move data. To load the result of a query, open **Transfer**, pick the same connection, and choose **SQL query** as the source extract, then paste the SELECT. **Stored procedure** runs one CALL or EXEC, spooled once. On **Destination**, **Query** runs one INSERT, MERGE, or UPDATE with binds and **Stored procedure** runs one CALL per row. Failed destination statements go to quarantine. CDC, SCD Type 2, and Mirror refuse callable destination writes. A query that worked here still goes through Validate.

chunks.doc_title: Job space, Trust Report, and reversibility
chunks.text:
Open Job space
Go to **Operations → Jobs**. The list shows each run's route, sync mode, rows, verification, and time. Filter by status, source, destination, mode, or verification, or search by table. Click a run to open it. The tabs are **Detail**, **Mapping**, **Trust Report**, **Reversibility**, and **Log**, plus **Quarantine** when rows were held back.
Jobs: the sales_orders → DW_DEMO run at the top, Full append, 5,100 rows, Verified.

chunks.doc_title: Job space, Trust Report, and reversibility
chunks.text:
Trust Report
The Trust Report reads both systems after the write. For the Snowflake run: 5,100 rows in the source, 5,100 in the destination, full checksum, Match. Under **How sure is this?** every row was compared.

Delivery is at-least-once, and CDC is at-least-once upsert unless a route proves otherwise.
Trust Report for the Snowflake run: 5,100 on each side, full checksum Match.

chunks.doc_title: Job space, Trust Report, and reversibility
chunks.text:
Reversibility
The **Reversibility** tab answers whether the destination can give the source values back. On the Snowflake run all 11 columns are invertible. `order_id` keeps `BIGINT` and the text columns widen to `VARCHAR`, so the rollback is **Restore from destination**.
Snowflake run: every column invertible, rollback by restoring from the destination.

chunks.doc_title: Job space, Trust Report, and reversibility
chunks.text:
Procedure: sign off a run
Sign-off records who accepted the evidence for a run.
Check the evidence
Scroll the Trust Report to **Evidence behind this report**. For the Snowflake run it shows reconciliation **Passed**, assurance **Full checksum**, and trust score **100**, plus whether a protection or transform proof applied. **Open Gate-8 proof** shows the read-back itself.
Where: Trust Report → Evidence behind this report
Sign for your role
Click **Go to sign-off**. **Engineering**, **Data owner**, and **Compliance** each sign the same report version. Choose your role, add a note on what you checked, and click **Sign as** your role. Each approval goes to the audit log. Once every required role has signed, the evidence pack is signed with the workspace proof key. **Download report (.md)** saves it for the audit file.
Where: Go to sign-off → Sign as …

chunks.doc_title: Job space, Trust Report, and reversibility
chunks.text:
Procedure: work through quarantine
Quarantined rows were held back with the column, value, and reason. They were not dropped.
Open the job
A run with held-back rows shows a non-zero rejected count and opens on the **Quarantine** tab.
Where: Operations → Jobs → select run
Read each row
Each entry shows the column, the value, the rule it failed, and when. Export the list if someone else needs to fix the source.
Where: Job detail → Quarantine
Fix and replay
Fix the map or the source, then replay the quarantined rows into the same destination, or resume the run from its checkpoint. A schedule fails the same way until the route is fixed.
Where: Fix the route → Replay or Resume
Tip: A run that completed with quarantine still wrote the clean rows. The Trust Report counts the held-back rows, so they are never missing from the totals.

Where enterprise settings live
Signed-in **admins** open **System → Settings**. Tabs include General, Security, Enterprise, SSO, Team, Notifications, AI Models, API Keys, and Audit Logs. The top-bar workspace switcher (and the picker on Team / Enterprise / Notifications) is one live workspace — switching it reloads each tab. Day-to-day operators usually stay on Connectors, Transfer, Schedules, and Jobs.
System → Settings: General, Security, Enterprise, SSO, Team, Notifications, AI Models, API Keys, and Audit Logs.

Procedure: configure SSO
Use SAML 2.0 (Okta / Azure AD / OneLogin) or OIDC (Google / Auth0 / Azure AD).
Open Settings → SSO
Choose SAML or OIDC. Paste IdP metadata URL or upload metadata XML. Map roles if your IdP sends group claims.
Where: System → Settings → SSO
Test, then Save
Run Test login with a pilot user. On success you see SSO ready. Save to enforce SSO for the tenant.
Where: SSO → Test · Save
Tip: Keep a break-glass admin account path documented with IT before enforcing SSO-only.

Team roles
Open **Settings → Team** to invite members by email and assign one of three roles (Viewer / Editor / Admin). The workspace picker on this tab is the same live workspace as the top bar — member lists refresh while the tab is open.
Viewer — inspect Jobs, proof, and connectors (no execute)
Editor — create connectors, run Transfer Studio and Schedules (an Admin manages members)
Admin — SSO, BYOK, Enterprise tab, API keys, grant Admin roles

BYOK, region, and audit
Settings → Enterprise sets tenant name, custom domain, data region, session timeout, and an IP allowlist for the custom domain. Optional BYOK wraps connector secrets with your KMS key. Settings → Audit Logs lists mapping decisions, job runs, quarantine events, and MCP calls for SOC 2 / GDPR / HIPAA review. Settings → Security downloads the Security posture report for procurement.

Authentication
Bearer tokens scoped to workspace. `$TENANT_ORIGIN` is the host in the browser address bar (the path is `/api/v1`). A workspace API key from **Settings → API Keys** is the same credential MCP uses. Its role decides what it may change. Enterprise uses SSO-backed service accounts.
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$TENANT_ORIGIN/api/v1/connectors"

Core endpoints
Catalog, preflight, run, and job status endpoints mirror Transfer Studio behavior.
Canonical prefix is /api/v1 — see docs/API_VERSIONING.md for deprecation policy
GET /api/v1/connectors — list with transfer-ready status
POST /api/v1/preflight — run the nine core gates plus the policy gates the route needs
POST /api/v1/transfer/run — execute governed load
GET /api/v1/connectors/jobs/{id} — status, quarantine, reconciliation
Runs started from the API appear in Jobs next to Studio runs, with the same Trust Report.

Webhooks
Subscribe to job.completed, job.failed, and pipeline.quarantine_threshold (schedule) events. Payloads include job ID, gate results, and reconciliation summary — no row payloads unless explicitly configured.
POST /api/v1/webhooks
{ "url": "https://your.app/hooks/datawrap", "events": ["job.completed"] }

What is quarantine?
Rows that fail validation during load are isolated with the column, value, and reason — never silently dropped. Open Operations → Jobs → Quarantine on the run to inspect or export them.
Quarantine and proof live on the job. Open the run in Job space to see held-back rows.

Who can run transfers?
Editors and Admins can create connectors and run Transfer Studio and Schedules. Viewers can open Jobs and read Trust Reports and quarantine. Roles are assigned under Settings → Team (Viewer, Editor, Admin — there is no Owner role) and can come from IdP group claims when SSO is configured.

Do schedules skip preflight?
No. Every scheduled run uses the same Validate gates and post-load read-back as a manual transfer. A failing gate blocks the write, and a finding that needs a person parks the schedule with the reason until the route is fixed.

chunks.section_title: How is data protected in transit and at rest?
chunks.text:
How is data protected in transit and at rest?
Connectors use TLS to sources and destinations. Secrets are encrypted at rest (optional customer BYOK). Quarantine replaces silent drops; post-load checksums prove what landed. Download the Security posture report from Settings → Security for procurement questionnaires.

chunks.section_title: How is Datawrap different from ETL scripts?
chunks.text:
How is Datawrap different from ETL scripts?
Columns are mapped by meaning with a confidence score, Validate stops a bad load before it writes, bad rows go to quarantine instead of being coerced quietly, and the destination is read back and compared after every load. SSO, roles, and audit logs come built in.
